question.prompt: Roy bought a new battery-gasoline hybrid car. On a trip the car ran exclusively on its battery for the first \(40\) miles, then ran exclusively on gasoline for the rest of the trip, using gasoline at a rate of \(0.02\) gallons per mile. On the whole trip he averaged \(55\) miles per gallon. How long was the trip in miles?

solutions.explanation:
Convert the gasoline consumption rate to miles per gallon:
\[
1\div0.02=50.
\]
Thus each gallon supplies \(50\) gasoline-powered miles. The whole-trip average is \(55\) miles per gallon, so the total distance exceeds the gasoline-powered distance by \(55-50=5\) miles for each gallon used.

That excess distance is exactly the \(40\) battery-powered miles. Therefore the car used
\[
40\div5=8\text{ gallons}.
\]
At the whole-trip average, the total distance was
\[
55\cdot8=440\text{ miles}.
\]
Indeed, \(8\) gallons cover \(400\) gasoline-powered miles, which together with the first \(40\) miles gives \(440\). The answer is \(\boxed{440}\), choice C.
solutions.title: Compare miles per gallon

solutions.explanation:
Let \(L\) be the trip length in miles. The stated finite miles-per-gallon average requires positive gasoline use, so \(L>40\). The gasoline-powered portion was \(L-40\) miles and consumed \(0.02(L-40)\) gallons.

An average of \(55\) miles per gallon means total distance equals \(55\) times the gasoline consumed. Hence
\[
L=55\cdot0.02(L-40)=1.1(L-40).
\]
Expanding and collecting terms gives
\[
L=1.1L-44,
\qquad 0.1L=44,
\qquad L=440.
\]
This value meets \(L>40\). It gives \(400\) gasoline-powered miles and \(0.02\cdot400=8\) gallons, so the average is \(440/8=55\) miles per gallon. The answer is \(\boxed{440}\), choice C.
